# Introduction

Starting one's first year at university brings quite a lot of
challenges. Students often move-out of their family homes, have to get
acquainted with a new environment, navigate new social contexts and
learn how to study more independently than in high school. Challenges
are especially present for students whose parents or guardians have not
enjoyed higher education themselves, as these students often lack the
practical support of someone who can assist them with navigating through
this new type of environment. These students not only face structural
inequalities that make them less prepared for the academic world
[@melian2026], but once entering college, they are also confronted with
a different type of world than what their family has prepared them for,
with different cultural expectations that give them a harder time
accessing the right skills, knowledge and resources needed to navigate
this world [@phillips2020 @stephens2014].

These students often experience a lack of social support within
universities and feel less like they belong there than students with
parents who have enjoyed university [@Janke2024 @Wittner2023]. This,
while a positive correlation exists between belonging, motivation and
enjoyment and a combination of these three affects the academic
achievement of students [@Pedler2022]. Thus, while these students are
already facing more challenges than others at universities, their
chances of better academic achievement are also affected by how much
they feel like they belong.

This does, however, not mean that all first generation students
experience the same level of difficulties at university. This also
depends on, for example, what their network at university looks like in
terms of socio-emotional support and instrumental support
[@Wittner2023]. What especially seems to be of importance is what the
friendship network of these students looks like. Melian et al. (2025)
show that for first-generation students, their mental and social
well-being was consistently linked to their friendship networks, while
this was not the case for other student groups.

However, there are differences in the type of friendship networks that
are positive for social well-being. [@Wittner2023] shows that the type
of network in terms of closeness affects how FGS manage at universities
and what influence it has on social well-being. Additionally, there can
be questioned how friendship-network similarity influences the
well-being of students. For example, in terms of racial diversity, it is
shown that for white students, there is a benefit in developing more
diverse friendships, while this is not necessarily the case for students
with a migration background [@Janke2024][@Salusky2024]. In the more
general population, it is shown that there are benefits to having a more
heterogeneous rather than a homogeneous network, as it leads to higher
levels of social well-being [@ramos2024]. Though, while in the more
general population it seems to lead to more positive effects, for first
generation students, this does not necessarily seem to be the case. For
this group, a more socioeconomically diverse network is linked to lower
levels of social well-being. They are likely facing more and different
challenges in these heterogeneous contexts, as they are navigating
between multiple cultural contexts and managing feelings of mismatch
[@melian2026 @phillips2020 @stephens2014].

Previous studies have thus already looked into the relationship between
friendship diversity and social well-being for students with parents
that do not have a university background. However, these students lack
the social network perspective that this study will take into account.
For example, Ramos et al. (2024) mention that their study is limited by
the fact that friendship is a subjective experience. A social network
perspective allows us to look into whether friendships are
*reciprocated*, meaning that if you see someone as your friend, there
can be also considered whether you see this person as a friend. Taking
this into account potentially yield a more complete picture between
diversity in friendship networks and social well-being, as it is likely
that answered friendships make someone feel more socially satisfied than
one-directed friendships.

Additionally, while Melian et al. (2025) have already looked into the
influence of a socioeconomically diverse network on social satisfaction
of first generation students, they did not take into account the
interdependencies that a social network analysis can take into account.
This perspective allows us to look into influence effects of social
networks, because the people with whom we form social relations
influence our attitudes, behaviours and also future relations [@SNASS].
For this study, that means that a social network perspective allows us
to control for assimilation effects of social satisfaction, meaning that
the social satisfaction ratings of students befriended with each other
may become more alike over time.

Thus, a social network perspective allows us to look into this topic in
new and different ways than previous studies have done and different
questions emerge from this. The study aims to answer three research
questions:
1.  "To what extent is the MLC network segregated based on parental education level?"
2.  "To what extent do reciprocated friendships among students with
    parents with the same educational level occur?"
3.  "To what extent do reciprocated friendships affect students' social
    satisfaction throughout the year?"
4.  "To what extent do reciprocated friendships among students with
    parents with the same education level affect their social
    satisfaction throughout the year?"
